name: Gewürztraminer

lines.s10: Gewürztraminer is the perfumed white of Alsace: lychee, rose petal and ginger, rich and soft, often with a touch of sweetness.
lines.s20: Gewürztraminer is a pink skinned grape that makes a deep gold, heady white, at home in Alsace. It smells of lychee, rose petal and ginger, feels rich and soft in the mouth, and is often just off dry.
lines.s45: Gewürztraminer announces itself before the glass reaches you. It is a pink skinned grape, and its home is Alsace, in the east of France. It smells of lychee, rose petal and ginger, and it is full and soft, low in acidity and often just off dry. The cellar keeps out of the way: no new oak, only ripe fruit. Alsace tends to be rich and heady, while California's cool coast is usually lighter and fresher. Pour it with washed rind cheese, foie gras or a fragrant Thai curry. Gewürz is the German word for spice, and Traminer is named for Tramin, a village in the Italian Alps.
lines.sale: Gewürztraminer is the white for fragrant, spiced food: all lychee and rose petal, with a soft, rich feel. I would pour it with the curry, or with a ripe washed rind cheese at the end.

glass.lead: Lychee, rose petal and ginger on a full, oily, low acid frame, deep gold and often just off dry.

ladder.where: Alsace, Alto Adige, the Anderson Valley and Marlborough

glass.structure: Dry to off dry, sometimes sweet. Acidity low, alcohol high, body full, with an oily texture and a faintly bitter finish.

old.where: Alsace above all; Alto Adige; Germany's Pfalz and Baden
old.glass: Alsace tends to be deep gold, full and oily, often off dry: lychee, rose petal, ginger and clove with low acidity, high alcohol and a faintly bitter finish. Alto Adige is usually nearer dry.
old.cellar: Picked late and very ripe, fermented in steel or large old casks with no new oak. The sweet late harvests are Vendanges Tardives and Sélection de Grains Nobles.

new.where: California's Anderson Valley, the Finger Lakes, Washington, New Zealand and Chile
new.glass: Typically paler, lighter and fresher: lychee, rose petal and pink grapefruit at lower alcohol, with a little more acidity and often less sweetness; most are dry to off dry.
new.cellar: Usually fermented cool in steel to guard the perfume and bottled young; a few late harvest wines are made.

contrast.why: Alsace lies dry and sunny behind the Vosges, with a long autumn, so the grape hangs late and turns rich, strong and soft. New World growers often choose cool sites, by a cold coast or far south, and seek freshness.
contrast.blur: Alsace also makes taut, dry wines and Alto Adige's stay near dry, while Gisborne's are often oily and just off dry, as Alsace's are.
contrast.call: Deep gold, oily weight and sweetness at high alcohol lean Alsace; a paler, fresher wine at lower alcohol leans New World.

service.temp: 45 to 50 degrees Fahrenheit, 7 to 10 degrees Celsius; the sweet late harvest wines a little colder.
service.glass: A white wine glass; a small glass for the sweet late harvest wines.
service.decant: Usually unnecessary: serve it fresh and cold from the bottle.
service.age: Most within three to eight years; Vendanges Tardives and Sélection de Grains Nobles keep far longer.

with.dish: Munster and other washed rind cheeses
with.why: the wine's perfume and weight match the pungent rind
soft, off dry fruit sits easily with chilli and coconut
a rich, off dry wine meets the richness
off dry fruit cools the cayenne and stands up to the smoke

labels.means: Late harvest, in Alsace: very ripe grapes and a rich wine, usually sweet.
Alsace's sweet wine from grapes shrivelled by noble rot, picked over several passes.
A named, classed vineyard of Alsace; Gewurztraminer is one of the four grapes most of them are kept for.
The French spelling, with no umlaut, as Alsace prints it.
The grape's Italian name, seen on bottles from Alto Adige and Trentino.

guest.a: Often a little. Many from Alsace are off dry, and the rich texture and low acidity make even a dry one taste sweeter than it is. Late harvest bottles are properly sweet.
Gewürz is German for spice, and Traminer is an old grape named for Tramin, a village in the Italian Alps. Think of it as the perfumed Traminer.

guest.q: Why is the wine so deep in colour?
guest.a: The grape's skins are pink, not green, and a little of that colour reaches the wine, which pours deep gold, sometimes with a coppery glint.

compare.tell: Muscat is grapey, with orange blossom, lighter and less oily; Gewürztraminer is lychee, rose petal and ginger on a fuller, softer frame.
Torrontés shares the rose perfume but is lighter and fresher, with a bitter finish; Gewürztraminer is fuller, oilier and lower in acidity.
Viognier is apricot and honeysuckle, with no lychee or ginger; Gewürztraminer adds rose petal and lychee and is often off dry.

cards.front: Gewürztraminer: what does the name mean, and where is it at home?
cards.back: Gewürz is German for spice; Traminer is named for Tramin in Alto Adige. Its home on a wine list is Alsace, where it is one of the four noble grapes.

cards.front: Gewürztraminer blind: Alsace or the New World, what tips it?
cards.back: Deep gold, oily weight, heady lychee and rose with some sweetness at high alcohol lean Alsace. A paler, fresher wine at lower alcohol leans New World, from a cool site such as the Anderson Valley.

cards.front: Gewürztraminer in the glass: which marks give it away?
cards.back: Lychee, rose petal, an oily full body and low acidity, often with a little sweetness and a faintly bitter finish.

questions.q: Two glasses of Gewürztraminer are poured blind. The first is deep gold, oily and off dry, heady with lychee and rose at high alcohol. The second is paler, lighter, fresher and nearly dry. Which pair of origins fits, in that order?
questions.exp: Deep colour, oily weight, sweetness and high alcohol mark Alsace, where the grape ripens late and fully. Cool New World sites such as Marlborough tend to give a lighter, fresher, drier wine.

questions.q: A guest orders a pungent Munster to finish and asks for a white that can stand up to it. Which grape do you suggest?
questions.exp: Alsace pours its own perfumed, full bodied Gewürztraminer with Munster: the wine's weight and scent match the cheese. The other three are light, quiet whites that the rind would bury.

questions.q: A guest reads Vendanges Tardives on a bottle of Alsace Gewurztraminer and asks what it means. What do you answer?
opts: A late harvest wine, rich and usually sweet
A dry wine aged in new oak
A sparkling wine made in the bottle
A wine from a single classed vineyard
questions.exp: Vendanges Tardives means late harvest: very ripe grapes and a rich wine, usually sweet. A single classed vineyard is shown as Alsace Grand Cru, and sparkling Alsace is Crémant.

report: Mode contrast, as the plan fixes it. The New World side is hedged: the New Zealand trade body says most of its wines are dry to off dry, and the Anderson Valley growers tie the grape to a cool, coastal climate; lighter and crisper is the typical bottle, not a rule.
The say line is the Court's own, guh-VURTS-trah-mee-ner.
Alto Adige is called nearer dry and not light: its consortium says the wines generally hold five to ten grams of sugar a litre, with high alcohol and low acidity.
The ladder keeps Alsace on the cool rung, as the Court's grid read does; Gisborne and the Columbia Valley stand as moderate.
The Régionale row's aroma line says baking spice, a family word; the entry names ginger, clove, allspice and cinnamon, as the reviewed profile and the Alto Adige consortium do.
The gumbo stands on the Court's grid read, which names Creole dishes for this grape.
Left out: that the grape is an aromatic, pink skinned mutation of Savagnin, read only in general references in this session; and California late harvest wines, for want of a regional source.
The sources were read through search results; this session could not open the hosts directly.

checked.verdict: Sound after seven fixes. The Alsace notes (lychee, passion fruit, mango, rose, the spices), the New Zealand style and the naming of Traminer for Tramin were confirmed.
changed: lines.s45: Traminer comes from Tramin is now Traminer is named for Tramin. The name is the village's; where the grape arose is disputed, and one reference calls the Alto Adige origin a myth.

worlds.contrast.new.glass, the call, the second card and the worlds question: crisper and a little more acidity are taken out. New Zealand's own trade body calls its Gewürztraminer full bodied, smooth and subtle in acidity, typically dry to off dry. The New World side is now paler, lighter, fresher and less sweet, though still soft in acidity.
worlds.contrast.new.cellar: under the grape's own name is taken out. Alsace prints the grape on the label too, so it parts nothing.

worlds.contrast.why: New World growers often choose cool sites. The plain statement was false of Washington's Columbia Valley, which the entry itself lists; and cooler sites read as cooler than Alsace, which the entry's own ladder and the Court's grid read call cool.
questions[0].opts: three of the four options ended on then Alsace, so the key stood out by its form. Alsace and Marlborough now each stand in three options.
labels[1].means: Sélection de Grains Nobles is picked over several passes, not berry by berry.
food.with[3].why: the fruit cools the cayenne and stands up to the smoke; it cannot cool smoke.
open: The lint's three notes on the word spice were read and left: each gives the meaning of Gewürz, where the family is the point.
The ladder calls Gisborne moderate, as a maritime region is classed against the world; the Codex's own Gisborne record calls it a warm coast, against the rest of New Zealand.
Alto Adige at five to ten grams of sugar a litre is the author's reading of the consortium, which could not be opened from this session.
